newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.N. may be pushed into peace enforcement role.
newsitem.headline: U.N. may be pushed into peace enforcement role.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council may be forced to impose peace as well as keep it when handling major headaches such as the collapse of state power in parts of Zaire, diplomats and experts said on Wednesday.

Marcel Broisard, executive director of the United Nations Institute of Training and Research, told reporters the failure of several recent peacekeeping missions may make U.N. members reluctant about joining future peace operations.
"It (will) not be peacekeeping, it would be peace enforcement. We have to clearly define the mandate. This is a big dilemma," Broisard said.
"A failed state is a problem we have to deal with," said the permanent representative of Japan to the U.N., Hisashi Owada.
Armed groups in these countries "don't often wear uniforms to identify themselves. They don't abide by the rules of the game in terms of the rules of war. They have no central authority," Owada said.

Tommy Koh, director of the Institute of Policy Studies in Singapore, said the U.N. had never faced these types of problems before and the international community was still groping for solutions to them.
"The U.N. is really faced with a whole new challenge," Koh said. "We are in a whole new era. We must think creatively and constructively of a new modality for operating in this area."
The three speakers co-chaired a conference in Singapore to review troubled U.N. peacekeeping missions in the former Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Liberia and Somalia.

The United Nations has found itself in trouble in several missions, which floundered after peacekeepers found themselves being shot at, as in Sarajevo and Somalia, or powerless to prevent massacres. Hundreds of thousands of people were killed in a wave of genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
Koh said quick action by the U.N. or even the United States could have headed off the genocide in Rwanda.
"In a collapsed state like Somalia or Rwanda, the problem is that the U.N. thought they could send a peacekeeping operation. But the peacekeeping troops have no peace to keep," Boisard said.
A similar situation has developed in Zaire, where a disorganised government army is fighting rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
The rebels control a substantial portion of the country's northeast. Aid workers said on Tuesday Zairean troops were engaged in looting in the town of Kindu, panicking residents in the area.
